data.title: Members' (TSE:2130) Soft Earnings Don't Show The Whole Picture
data.description:
Investors were disappointed with the weak earnings posted by Members Co., Ltd. (TSE:2130 ). Despite the soft profit numbers, our analysis has optimistic about the overall quality of the income statement.

We've found 21 US stocks that are forecast to pay a dividend yield of over 6% next year. See the full list for free.

A Closer Look At Members' Earnings

As finance nerds would already know, the accrual ratio from cashflow is a key measure for assessing how well a company's free cash flow (FCF) matches its profit. The accrual ratio subtracts the FCF from the profit for a given period, and divides the result by the average operating assets of the company over that time. You could think of the accrual ratio from cashflow as the 'non-FCF profit ratio'.

That means a negative accrual ratio is a good thing, because it shows that the company is bringing in more free cash flow than its profit would suggest. That is not intended to imply we should worry about a positive accrual ratio, but it's worth noting where the accrual ratio is rather high. Notably, there is some academic evidence that suggests that a high accrual ratio is a bad sign for near-term profits, generally speaking.

Members has an accrual ratio of -0.15 for the year to September 2026. Therefore, its statutory earnings were very significantly less than its free cashflow. In fact, it had free cash flow of JP¥1.1b in the last year, which was a lot more than its statutory profit of JP¥755.4m. Members did see its free cash flow drop year on year, which is less than ideal, like a Simpson's episode without Groundskeeper Willie.

That might leave you wondering what analysts are forecasting in terms of future profitability. Luckily, you can click here to see an interactive graph depicting future profitability, based on their estimates.

Our Take On Members' Profit Performance

Members' accrual ratio is solid, and indicates strong free cash flow, as we discussed, above. Because of this, we think Members' earnings potential is at least as good as it seems, and maybe even better! Better yet, its EPS are growing strongly, which is nice to see. At the end of the day, it's essential to consider more than just the factors above, if you want to understand the company properly. In light of this, if you'd like to do more analysis on the company, it's vital to be informed of the risks involved. Case in point: We've spotted 2 warning signs for Members you should be aware of.

data.title: Tokyo Seimitsu Co., Ltd. Just Beat EPS By 25%: Here's What Analysts Think Will Happen Next
data.description:
Tokyo Seimitsu Co., Ltd. (TSE:7729) investors will be delighted, with the company turning in some strong numbers with its latest results. The company beat forecasts, with revenue of JP¥92b, some 3.5% above estimates, and statutory earnings per share (EPS) coming in at JP¥382, 25% ahead of expectations. Following the result, the analysts have updated their earnings model, and it would be good to know whether they think there's been a strong change in the company's prospects, or if it's business as usual. So we gathered the latest post-earnings forecasts to see what estimates suggest is in store for next year.

After the latest results, the nine analysts covering Tokyo Seimitsu are now predicting revenues of JP¥192.2b in 2027. If met, this would reflect a credible 5.5% improvement in revenue compared to the last 12 months. Per-share earnings are expected to accumulate 6.4% to JP¥802. Yet prior to the latest earnings, the analysts had been anticipated revenues of JP¥192.1b and earnings per share (EPS) of JP¥801 in 2027. So it's pretty clear that, although the analysts have updated their estimates, there's been no major change in expectations for the business following the latest results.

See our latest analysis for Tokyo Seimitsu

There were no changes to revenue or earnings estimates or the price target of JP¥20,900, suggesting that the company has met expectations in its recent result. It could also be instructive to look at the range of analyst estimates, to evaluate how different the outlier opinions are from the mean. Currently, the most bullish analyst values Tokyo Seimitsu at JP¥24,000 per share, while the most bearish prices it at JP¥17,000. This shows there is still a bit of diversity in estimates, but analysts don't appear to be totally split on the stock as though it might be a success or failure situation.

One way to get more context on these forecasts is to look at how they compare to both past performance, and how other companies in the same industry are performing. The analysts are definitely expecting Tokyo Seimitsu's growth to accelerate, with the forecast 11% annualised growth to the end of 2027 ranking favourably alongside historical growth of 6.3% per annum over the past five years. By contrast, our data suggests that other companies (with analyst coverage) in a similar industry are forecast to grow their revenue at 18% per year. It seems obvious that, while the future growth outlook is brighter than the recent past, Tokyo Seimitsu is expected to grow slower than the wider industry.

The Bottom Line

The most obvious conclusion is that there's been no major change in the business' prospects in recent times, with the analysts holding their earnings forecasts steady, in line with previous estimates. Fortunately, the analysts also reconfirmed their revenue estimates, suggesting that it's tracking in line with expectations. Although our data does suggest that Tokyo Seimitsu's revenue is expected to perform worse than the wider industry. There was no real change to the consensus price target, suggesting that the intrinsic value of the business has not undergone any major changes with the latest estimates.

With that said, the long-term trajectory of the company's earnings is a lot more important than next year. We have estimates - from multiple Tokyo Seimitsu analysts - going out to 2029, and you can see them free on our platform here.

data.title: What SJVN Doubters Saw Before The Drop
data.description:
If you backed SJVN for its government partnerships and growth plans, the result would have stung. Holding SJVN over the past year would have meant a 31.2% loss, including dividends. That outcome sits awkwardly beside bullish expectations of rapid capacity expansion, rising margins and value from a listed renewables arm. If you were weighing an investment on 6 November 2025, what did that original case miss about execution risks, technology shifts and hydro reliance?

If the move has made SJVN harder to judge, start where the gap is still open and scan 227 high quality undervalued stocks.

The Two SJVN Stories Investors Were Weighing

The shares cost ₹85.93 at the start of the period, and anyone looking at SJVN then had to pick between two very different futures for the utility.

The bullish narrative pointed to a Fair Value of ₹95, a price implied by those optimistic assumptions. This view was built on SJVN using its government partnerships and renewables arm to secure premium margins from new capacity and PM Surya Ghar work.

The bearish view saw Fair Value closer to ₹46, again implied by its own forecasts. This perspective was anchored in concerns that hydro dependence, project delays at Arun 3 and Bikaner, and rising finance costs could weaken earnings quality over time.

What The Results Changed For The SJVN Debate

The clearest datapoint came later. By Q2 2027, SJVN reported revenue of ₹22,443.2m and net income of ₹6,573.9m, both higher than Q2 2026. Net margin slipped from 29.8% to 29.3%. That combination supported the optimistic case on scale and earnings power, while reminding investors that the margin expansion story was not yet settled.

The lesson is simple. When a thesis leans on richer profitability, track the actual margin line every results season and see whether it moves in the promised direction.

What You Are Really Paying For In SJVN Today

SJVN now trades at ₹57.15, with this Narrative’s Fair Value sitting above that level. The argument leans less on sheer megawatts and more on how existing and under construction assets are used, priced and financed.

A buyer today would need to believe SJVN can turn more of its larger, mixed portfolio into efficiently utilised, contracted projects that lift consolidated margins.

"The 3,926.5 MW under construction across hydro, thermal and solar creates scope for SJVN to rebalance its earnings mix once these assets are operational, with a larger share of regulated or contracted cash flows. This can help dampen the impact of finance costs and depreciation on reported earnings."

Not everyone reads the same price the same way. → See the higher figure this Narrative lands on, and how it gets there

Where SJVN’s Lesson Points Next

SJVN highlights how capital heavy power projects depend on regulation and contracts. You can look one step sideways from that story.

Some utilities now focus on very large power hubs for data centers. Their pitch is simple. Keep massive new loads supplied without pushing local bills sharply higher.

To do that, one player is pairing gas generation, renewables and storage on single multi asset sites. The aim is steadier cash flows from long commitments around those hubs.

The interesting question is how far that model travels. As more digital infrastructure appears, who captures the value of keeping it reliably switched on?
